title: Significant, and still a fluke?
hook: A study's result passes the 5% test. How likely is it that the effect isn't real?

knows: what 'significant at 5%' means for one test (how-surprising-is-sixty)
doesNotKnow: that the share of significant results that are false depends on how many tested ideas were true to begin with, and can be far above 5%

misconception: A result significant at 5% has about a 95% chance of being real.
objective: The learner can explain that the 5% is the fluke rate among ideas that do nothing, so when true ideas are rare, flukes can be a large share of all passing results.

claims.text: With 1,000 ideas, 10% true, 80% detection and a 5% fluke rate, 80 real effects and 45 flukes pass, so 36% of passes are flukes; 900 of the 1,000 ideas are duds.
claims.source: Arithmetic: tp = 1,000 x 0.10 x 0.8 = 80; fp = 900 x 0.05 = 45; 45/125 = 36.0%. Brief 56 check (company/domains/briefs/checks/probability-round4-check.mjs). Demo.tsx counts(10).
claims.note: Derivation re-run in node (own copy of counts()): 1,000 x 0.10 x 0.8 = 80 real, round(900 x 0.05) = 45 flukes, 45/125 = 36.0%; marked() draws exactly 80 rings and 45 crosses. Brief check script agrees. No source needed.

claims.text: With 1% true, 86% of passes are flukes (8 real, 50 flukes drawn); with 50% true, 6% (400 real, 25 flukes).
claims.source: Arithmetic: 1%: tp 8, fp 990 x 0.05 = 49.5, drawn as 50 on the grid (Math.round); 49.5/57.5 = 86.1%, 50/58 = 86.2%, both 86% at the stage's whole-percent rounding. 50%: tp 400, fp 25, 25/425 = 5.9% -> 6%. Brief 56 check.
claims.note: Derivation re-run: 1%: 8 real, 49.5 drawn as 50 (Math.round), 50/58 = 86.2% (unrounded 86.1%), both 86%; 50%: 400 and 25, 5.88% -> 6%. Grid draws exactly those counts.

claims.text: The 5% threshold limits flukes among ideas that do nothing; it does not give the chance that a passing result is real. How far to trust a significant result depends on how many tested ideas were likely true.
claims.source: Definition of a significance threshold: P(pass | dud) = 0.05. P(dud | pass) = P(pass | dud)P(dud) / P(pass), which depends on the prior share of true ideas (Bayes' rule); c1 and c2 are instances.
claims.note: Derivation (Bayes' rule): P(dud | pass) = 0.05 P(dud) / P(pass) depends on the prior share; c1 and c2 are instances. Recall check: 1 in 50 true gives 75% of passes as flukes, so 'could easily be a fluke' holds.

claims.text: The 80% catch rate and 5% fluke rate are the stage's settings, not figures about any field.
claims.source: Lesson rule (brief 56 planned claim 4); stated on the stage caption 'Tests catch 80%; 5% of duds pass.'
claims.note: Convention, consistent: the caption 'Tests catch 80%; 5% of duds pass.' is on the stage and the code uses CATCH 0.8, FLUKE 0.05.

claims.text: (Not shown to the learner.) Optional context: Ioannidis (2005), 'Why most published research findings are false', PLoS Medicine 2(8): e124.

recall.question: In a field where only 1 in 50 tested ideas is true, a result passes a 5% significance test. Is it about 95% likely to be real?
options: No, it could easily be a fluke, because duds far outnumber true ideas
No, it is exactly 5% likely to be real
recall.why: The 5% is the fluke rate among duds. With 49 duds per true idea, flukes from that big pile can make up a large share of all passing results.
